subject: Economics
description: Demand-pull, cost-push, stagflation, hyperinflation, deflation, CPI vs WPI

questions.stem: INFLATION caused by RISING DEMAND in the economy is called:

options.option_text: Cost-push inflation (supply-side)
Demand-pull inflation (demand-side)
Hyperinflation (very rapid > 50%/mo)
Stagflation (stagnation + inflation)

questions.explanation: DEMAND-PULL INFLATION — 'too much money chasing too few goods'. Demand exceeds supply at current prices → prices rise. Causes: govt. spending, low interest rates, increased credit, expansion of money supply, consumer optimism. COST-PUSH INFLATION — input costs (oil, wages, raw materials) rise → producers pass costs on. STAGFLATION — high inflation + low growth + high unemployment (rare; 1970s OPEC oil shocks). HYPERINFLATION — extreme: Weimar Germany (1923), Zimbabwe (2008 — 79.6 BILLION % monthly!), Venezuela (recent).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Inflation in India is officially measured by:

options.option_text: Only the WPI (Wholesale Price Index) used
Mainly CPI (Consumer Price Index) since 2014
GDP deflator alone is the official measure
Stock-market index alone measures inflation

questions.explanation: India's inflation: from 2014, RBI uses CPI (Combined: rural + urban, ~46% food weightage; published by NSO/MoSPI). Earlier WPI (with very different weights — manufactured goods 64%, primary goods 22%, fuel 14%) was the main reference. WPI still tracked but CPI is the policy benchmark. CPI BASKET in India: Food + Beverages 46%, Housing 10%, Fuel + Light 7%, Clothing 7%, Health 6%, Education 4%, Pan + Tobacco 2%, Misc + Recreation. UPDATED periodically (current base 2012=100; revision in progress to 2024).
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Decreasing inflation rate (still positive figure)
Falling general price level (negative inflation)
Stable, zero inflation always for some periods
Rising prices in only one sector of economy

questions.explanation: DEFLATION — sustained DECREASE in general price level (inflation rate < 0). DISINFLATION = decrease in inflation RATE (rate still positive but smaller). REFLATION = bringing economy out of deflation back to normal. Why deflation is bad: consumers postpone purchases (waiting for cheaper prices) → demand falls → producers cut output / jobs → economy contracts (deflationary spiral). Japan suffered deflation 1990s-2010s ('Lost Decades'). Distractor 1 = disinflation. Distractor 3 = price stability.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: CORE INFLATION typically excludes which categories?

options.option_text: Manufactured goods + services
Food + fuel (most volatile)
Housing + clothing categories
Health + education services

questions.explanation: CORE INFLATION = headline inflation EXCLUDING food + fuel (the most volatile categories). Why exclude: food (weather, seasonality) + fuel (oil prices, geopolitical events) are highly variable, can mask underlying trend. Core inflation reveals UNDERLYING price pressure — better signal for monetary policy. Persistent high core inflation = entrenched inflation, harder to control. RBI looks at both headline + core CPI. (Some economists prefer 'sticky CPI' or 'trimmed mean CPI' — different ways to filter volatile components.)
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Lenders and savers benefit most from inflation
Borrowers (loans repaid in cheaper currency)
Pensioners on fixed income gain from inflation
Salaried employees with no salary rise also gain

questions.explanation: Inflation effects: BENEFITS BORROWERS — they repay loans in money worth less than at borrowing time (real value of loan eroded). HURTS LENDERS + SAVERS — interest income may not keep up with inflation; real returns fall (especially fixed-deposit holders with rate < inflation). HURTS PENSIONERS + fixed-income earners — purchasing power of pension declines. HURTS salaried (without inflation-linked increments). REAL ESTATE + GOLD often gain (inflation hedges). EQUITY can be a hedge over LONG term (stocks of companies with pricing power).
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: Stagnant prices + unemployment
Stagnant economy with rising inflation
High growth with low inflation
Recession with falling prices everywhere

questions.explanation: STAGFLATION = STAGnation (low or zero growth, high unemployment) + inFLATION (rising prices). Term coined by Iain Macleod (UK Chancellor) in 1965. RARE but very dangerous: standard Keynesian tools (rate cuts to boost growth) WORSEN inflation; tools to cut inflation (rate hikes) WORSEN unemployment. Famous case: 1973-75 OIL SHOCK — OPEC quadrupled oil prices → cost-push inflation + recession in West. India in 2010-13 saw mild stagflationary tendencies. Distractor 4 = recession + deflation = depression.

questions.stem: HYPERINFLATION is generally defined as inflation rate exceeding:

options.option_text: 10% per year (high inflation)
50% per month (extreme cases)
100% per year (severe inflation)
Any rise in prices monthly

questions.explanation: HYPERINFLATION — extreme inflation, typically defined (Cagan, 1956) as > 50% PER MONTH (~129× per year compounded). Famous cases: HUNGARY 1946 (inflation rate 4.19 × 10¹⁶% per month — worst ever; pengő replaced with forint at ratio 1 forint = 4 × 10²⁹ pengő). WEIMAR GERMANY 1923 (~30,000% per month; price doubled every ~3.7 days; people burning Marks for fuel cheaper than firewood). ZIMBABWE 2008 (89.7 sextillion % year-on-year peak; printed 100 trillion-dollar notes). VENEZUELA 2018 (~1,000,000% annual). Causes: usually massive money printing to cover deficit during crisis. Cure: replace currency, anchor to hard currency or gold.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: When the rate of inflation is declining but prices are still rising (not falling), the economy is experiencing:

options.option_text: Deflation — a sustained fall in the general price level
Disinflation — a falling rate of inflation, prices still rising
Stagflation — coexistence of high inflation with low growth
Reflation — policy-driven reversal of deflationary pressure

questions.explanation: Disinflation means the inflation rate is slowing down — prices still rise, just more slowly. This is fundamentally different from deflation (Option A), where prices actually fall. Stagflation (C) involves inflation combined with stagnant output; reflation (D) is a stimulus policy after a deflationary slump. Candidates frequently confuse disinflation with deflation, making A the most dangerous distractor here.

questions.stem: A rise in the price of crude oil in international markets pushes up fuel, transport and production costs domestically. This transmission of inflation is best described as:

options.option_text: Demand-pull inflation, triggered by excess domestic spending
Built-in inflation, caused by the domestic wage-price spiral
Imported inflation, arising from higher input costs sourced abroad
Structural inflation, rooted in long-run domestic supply bottlenecks

questions.explanation: Imported inflation occurs when price shocks originating in foreign markets — typically oil, metals, or food commodities — are transmitted into domestic costs and prices. India's recurring fuel-driven inflation episodes are classic examples. Demand-pull (A) originates from excess domestic demand; built-in inflation (B) is the wage-price spiral; structural (D) reflects domestic supply-side weaknesses like inadequate infrastructure.

questions.stem: Workers demand a 10% wage hike to cope with rising prices; firms raise product prices to recover higher wage costs; workers then demand further wage increases. This self-perpetuating cycle is the core mechanism of:

options.option_text: Demand-pull inflation, driven by surplus aggregate demand in markets
Structural inflation, caused by sectoral supply-side bottlenecks
Built-in inflation, powered by the wage-price spiral feedback loop
Open inflation, operating without any government price-control check

questions.explanation: Built-in (or inertial) inflation describes the wage-price spiral: past inflation causes workers to demand compensatory wage increases, which raises firms' costs, which raises prices, which triggers another wage demand round — a self-sustaining loop. Demand-pull (A) requires new excess demand to start; structural (B) stems from supply-side rigidities, not a wage-cost loop; open inflation (D) is a classification by government response, not by mechanism.

questions.stem: A government, after a period of recession and declining price levels, deliberately expands money supply and public expenditure to restore economic activity and nudge prices back upward. This policy stance is called:

options.option_text: Disinflation, which targets a reduction in the existing rate of inflation
Deflation, representing the natural downward movement of the price level
Stagflation, describing simultaneous stagnant growth and price inflation
Reflation, aimed at lifting depressed price levels back toward a target

questions.explanation: Reflation is the deliberate use of fiscal or monetary stimulus to push a below-target or falling price level back up after a deflationary episode or recession. It is policy-driven and intentional. Disinflation (A) is the slowing of an existing inflationary rate — the opposite context. Deflation (B) is the condition being cured, not the cure. Stagflation (C) is a descriptor of an adverse state, not a policy instrument.

questions.stem: In an economy where government price controls and rationing mask underlying excess money supply, the inflation is present but not visible in official price indices. This is termed:

options.option_text: Open inflation, where prices rise freely with no administrative ceiling
Creeping inflation, characterised by very slow but continuous price rises
Suppressed inflation, concealed by price controls and quantity rationing
Structural inflation, arising from long-run domestic supply-side failures

questions.explanation: Suppressed (or repressed) inflation exists when the monetary conditions for inflation are present — excess demand, rising money supply — but government-imposed price ceilings and rationing prevent prices from rising in official data. Once controls are lifted, the suppressed inflation surfaces suddenly. Open inflation (A) is the opposite: prices are free to adjust. Creeping (B) is a rate-classification. Structural (D) is a cause-based classification.

questions.stem: During 2009–2011, India's food-article wholesale prices surged at 15–20%, while manufactured goods inflation remained below 5%, creating a pronounced divergence in sectoral price behaviour. Former CEA Kaushik Basu used which specific term to describe this phenomenon?

options.option_text: Hyperinflation, where economy-wide prices exceed 50% monthly rise
Structural inflation, driven entirely by a domestic monetary overhang
Skewflation, where price pressure is concentrated in a specific sector
Stagflation, combining broad-based price surge with GDP output stagnation

questions.explanation: Kaushik Basu (then Chief Economic Adviser, Government of India) coined 'skewflation' to describe inflation that is skewed across sectors — sharply high in food but moderate elsewhere. It matters for policy because a blanket monetary tightening to curb food inflation would unfairly penalise the non-food sectors that did not experience the price surge. Structural inflation (B) is caused by supply-side rigidities but does not necessarily imply this sectoral skew; stagflation (D) requires output stagnation alongside inflation, which was not the India 2009–11 context.

questions.stem: In theory, which form of inflation is considered the LEAST economically distortionary, because rational agents can fully incorporate it into wage contracts, loan interest rates, and pricing decisions beforehand?

options.option_text: Unanticipated inflation, as market participants respond with contract revisions
Hyperinflation, since its extreme visibility forces immediate behavioural change
Stagflation, because price and output signals simultaneously inform agent choices
Anticipated inflation, as agents pre-adjust wages, rates, and prices accurately

questions.explanation: Anticipated (or expected) inflation is theoretically less harmful because economic agents — workers, lenders, firms — can incorporate the expected price rise into contracts in advance, preserving real values (real wages, real interest rates). The redistribution and misallocation effects associated with inflation largely disappear when expectations are accurate. Unanticipated inflation (A) causes arbitrary wealth transfers from creditors to debtors and misallocates resources. Hyperinflation (B) destroys price signals entirely. Stagflation (C) is a macroeconomic condition, not an expectations-based category.
